title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

reading.body:
Scammers used artificial intelligence to impersonate Terry Gross and other Fresh Air staff in personalized emails to public figures and authors. The emails offered interview opportunities with detailed references to the target's work and professional booking procedures, then requested payment of around $250 for supposed production costs. The system deployed at scale, reaching celebrities and journalists including Nikki Glaser, Amy Poehler, and Katie Couric.

This is an impersonation attack enabled by AI's ability to generate convincing, personalized messages cheaply. The failure occurred in the trust recipients placed in email communications that appeared to come from a known organization and matched the apparent sender's professional voice. It would have been caught by verification through legitimate organizational contacts, which experts recommended as a safeguard.

It is not established whether the scammers used a specific commercial AI tool or built their own system.

reports.title: ‘Too good to be true?’: No, WHYY’s Terry Gross did not personally email you to be a guest on ‘Fresh Air’
Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood

summary:
# Summary

Scammers are impersonating Terry Gross and other "Fresh Air" staff members to defraud public figures and authors. Recipients receive personalized emails claiming to offer interview opportunities on the popular NPR program, complete with detailed references to the target's work and professional booking procedures. However, the scam eventually requests payment, typically around $250, for supposed production costs. WHYY, NPR, and law enforcement are investigating these fraudulent messages, which have also targeted celebrities like comedians Nikki Glaser and Amy Poehler, as well as journalist Katie Couric.

Cybersecurity experts attribute the scam's effectiveness to artificial intelligence, which allows criminals to create highly convincing, personalized impersonations at minimal cost. Red flags include requests for payment, emails from suspicious addresses like terrygrossfreshair@gmail.com, and the implausibility of a major show's host handling personal logistics. WHYY confirmed it never charges guests for interviews. Experts recommend verifying requests through legitimate organizational contacts rather than responding to suspicious emails.
